### Problem: Alternating Subsequence {#sec-tp-p6-b}

::: {.p-statement}
$t$ test cases ($1 \le t \le 10^4$). Each: $n$ **non-zero** integers $a_1, \dots, a_n$ ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot10^5$, $-10^9 \le a_i \le 10^9$, $\sum n \le 2\cdot10^5$). Choose a subsequence with **no two adjacent elements of the same sign** that has the **maximum possible length**; among all of those, maximise the **sum**. Print that sum.

Source: [CF 1343C · Alternating Subsequence](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1343/C){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
"Maximum length first" decides the shape for you: signs split the array into maximal *same-sign runs*, and any alternating subsequence can take at most one element from each run (two from one run would sit adjacent with the same sign somewhere in between). Taking exactly one per run is the unique way to reach maximum length — so the only freedom left is *which* element of each run, and to maximise the sum you simply take the run's **maximum** (largest positive, or smallest-in-absolute-value negative, i.e. `max` either way). That is the group pointer of @sec-tp-runs/@sec-tp-p6-a with the chain test changed from "next value $= + 1$" to "next sign $=$ same".
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Enumerate subsequences.** Try every subset in order, keep those whose signs alternate, compare by (length, sum) lexicographically. $O(2^n n)$ — oracle only.
2. **Run maxima.** Scan left to right; at each run start $\mathit{i}$, let $\mathit{j}$ jump while the sign stays the same; add $\max(a[i..j])$; continue at $\mathit{j}+1$. $O(n)$.

**Invariant.** When the inner pointer stops at $\mathit{j}$, $[\mathit{i}, \mathit{j}]$ is a maximal same-sign run, runs partition the array in order, and the answer so far is the optimal (longest, then heaviest) choice restricted to the runs finished so far — runs are independent because any cross-run pick is automatically sign-alternating.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Enumerate all subsequences

::: {.form-next}
A depth-first recursion over "take or skip" at each index, with a last-sign check, compares candidates by the pair (length, sum) — length first, exactly as the statement orders the objectives. $O(2^n n)$; this is the checker, and the place the two-key comparison is spelled out honestly.

**"Subsequence" and the two-key comparison, in plain words.** A *subsequence* keeps the original order but may drop elements; the recursion decides, index by index, to *take* or *skip* $a[i]$, taking it only when its sign differs from the last one taken. The statement wants maximum **length** first and, among those, maximum **sum** — which is exactly what comparing the pair `(length, total)` does, because Python compares tuples left-to-right (length wins ties only when lengths are equal).

**Worked example.** $a = [1, 2, 3, -1, -2, 3]$. The longest alternating subsequences have length $3$ (one pick from each of the runs $[1,2,3]$, $[-1,-2]$, $[3]$); among those the heaviest is $[3, -1, 3]$ with sum $5$, so the oracle returns $5$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def alt_subseq_brute(a):                  # max by LENGTH, tie-broken by max sum
    n = len(a)
    best = [None]
    def rec(i, last_sign, length, total):
        if i == n:
            if best[0] is None or (length, total) > best[0]:
                best[0] = (length, total)
            return
        x = a[i]; sgn = 1 if x > 0 else -1
        if last_sign == 0 or sgn != last_sign:
            rec(i + 1, sgn, length + 1, total + x)
        rec(i + 1, last_sign, length, total)
    rec(0, 0, 0, 0)
    return best[0][1]
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - exponential oracle (small n only)
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
long long altSubseqBrute(const vector<long long>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    pair<long long, long long> best{-1, -1};   // (length, sum)
    for (int mask = 0; mask < (1 << n); ++mask) {
        long long len = 0, sum = 0, last = 0; bool ok = true;
        for (int i = 0; i < n && ok; ++i) if (mask >> i & 1) {
            long long sgn = a[i] > 0 ? 1 : -1;
            if (last != 0 && sgn == last) ok = false;
            last = sgn; ++len; sum += a[i];
        }
        if (ok && make_pair(len, sum) > best) best = {len, sum};
    }
    return best.second;
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `rec(i, last_sign, length, total)` is a depth-first search over "take or skip" at index $i$. `if last_sign == 0 or sgn != last_sign` lets us take $a[i]$ only when it flips the sign (or nothing is taken yet); the take-branch adds to `length` and `total`, and the unconditional `rec(i + 1, last_sign, length, total)` is the skip-branch. At `i == n` a full candidate is measured, and `(length, total) > best[0]` keeps the better one by the length-then-sum rule. Two branches per index over $n$ indices is $O(2^n)$ — fine as a checker for tiny arrays.

#### One maximum per same-sign run

::: {.form-next}
The greedy the length-first rule forces: jump a group pointer $\mathit{j}$ over each maximal same-sign run, take `max` of the run, move on. $O(n)$ with $O(1)$ extra space; the maximum *sum* is now a corollary of taking the maximum *length* — one independent choice per run.

**"Same-sign run", in plain words.** Split the array into maximal blocks of consecutive positives or consecutive negatives — the signs play the role that "consecutive integers" played in @sec-tp-p6-a. To get the longest alternating subsequence you take **exactly one** element per block (two from a block would repeat a sign), and to also maximise the sum that one should be the block's largest value. For a positive block `max` is the biggest number; for a negative block `max` is the one closest to zero (e.g. $\max(-1, -2) = -1$) — `max()` does the right thing either way.

**Worked example.** $a = [1, 2, 3, -1, -2, 3]$ has runs $[1,2,3]$, $[-1,-2]$, $[3]$ with maxima $3, -1, 3$, so the sum is $3 + (-1) + 3 = 5$ — matching the oracle, in one linear pass.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("alt", "runs")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-alt-subseq-runs
def alt_subseq(a):                        # sum of the max of each same-sign run
    total = 0; i = 0; n = len(a)
    while i < n:
        j = i
        while j + 1 < n and (a[j + 1] > 0) == (a[i] > 0):
            j += 1                        # still inside the same-sign run
        total += max(a[i:j + 1])
        i = j + 1
    return total

for _ in range(300):
    a = [random.randint(-5, 5) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 9))]
    a = [x if x != 0 else 1 for x in a]   # CF input has no zero
    assert alt_subseq(a) == alt_subseq_brute(a)
assert alt_subseq([1, 2, 3, -1, -2, 3]) == 5    # 3 + (-1) + 3
assert alt_subseq([2, 1, 3, 3]) == 3            # one positive run -> max
assert alt_subseq([1, 2, 3, -1, -2]) == 2       # the four CF samples
assert alt_subseq([-1, -2, -1, -3]) == -1
assert alt_subseq([-2, 8, 3, 8, -4, -15, 5, -2, -3, 1]) == 6
assert alt_subseq([1, -10**9, 1, -10**9, 1, -10**9]) == -2999999997
print("alt_subseq OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;
using ll = long long;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int T; cin >> T;
    while (T--) {
        int n; cin >> n;
        vector<ll> a(n);
        for (ll& x : a) cin >> x;
        ll ans = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; ) {
            int j = i;
            ll best = a[i];
            while (j + 1 < n && (a[j + 1] > 0) == (a[i] > 0)) best = max(best, a[++j]);
            ans += best;
            i = j + 1;
        }
        cout << ans << '\n';
    }
}
```
:::

**Reading it line by line.** `total, i = 0, 0` accumulates the answer run by run. For each run, `j = i` and the inner `while j + 1 < n and (a[j + 1] > 0) == (a[i] > 0): j += 1` races $\mathit{j}$ forward while the *sign* (whether a value is $> 0$) stays the same, so $[\mathit{i}, \mathit{j}]$ is a maximal same-sign block. `total += max(a[i:j + 1])` adds that block's single best pick, and `i = j + 1` starts the next block. Exactly the Summary-Ranges skeleton with a sign test instead of a $+1$ test — hence $O(n)$, one pass, and each run's choice is independent because crossing a boundary automatically alternates the sign.

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Enumerate all subsequences** is $O(2^n n)$ — $n$ up to $\sim 20$ only. **One maximum per same-sign run** is $O(n)$ per test case, $O(\sum n)$ overall, $O(n)$ space for the array (streaming keeps it $O(1)$). The sum can reach $2\cdot10^5 \cdot 10^9 = 2\cdot10^{14}$, so `long long` is mandatory (@sec-arr-cost); in Python the issue disappears.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- All one sign: one run, answer $= \max$ of the array — not the sum of all elements (a common wrong greedy that ignores the length-first rule).
- Negatives only, e.g. $[-5, -2, -9]$: the single run's maximum is $-2$; "maximum" means closest to zero, and `max()` already does the right thing.
- Zeros never appear ($a_i \ne 0$); if you generalise the code, decide whether $0$ counts as positive or negative and stay consistent — the sign test is `(x > 0)`, which files $0$ with the negatives.
:::

::: {.practice}
- Re-solve @sec-tp-p6-b, then explain out loud why "maximum length first" removes all interaction between runs — what makes the per-run choice independent?
- @sec-tp-p6-a (LC 228, Summary Ranges) — the identical group-pointer skeleton with a different chain test; diff the two loops line by line.
- [CF 1843B · Long Long](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1843/B){rating="800"} — the answer is the sum of absolute values, and the number of operations is the number of maximal runs of negatives (zeros do not break a run): the same group pointer, counting runs instead of taking maxima.
- Drop the length rule and maximise the sum alone: on $[2, 9, -100]$ the run greedy returns $-91$ but $[9]$ alone gives $9$ (chapter exercise 13). Explain which step of the proof needed the length rule.
:::
